To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the majority of patients in this study received facility-based rehabilitation, with a higher proportion of public recipients participating in home-based programs.

the majority of patients undergoing total knee and hip replacement are not referred to rehabilitation services and that those referred to rehabilitation services do not receive the recommended number of therapy sessions.

facility-based programs remain the most common form of rehabilitation for most knee and hip arthroplasties, with insurance status being an important determinant of care, and that development of evidence-based guidelines is needed to help resolve the evidence/practice gap and reduce unwarranted practice variations.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the rehabilitation of patients following knee or hip arthoplasty.
the provision of post-surgical rehabilitation for individuals with osteoarthritis of the hip or knee.
the rehabilitation of patients after total knee and total hip arthroplasties (TKA and THA).
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
facility-based rehabilitation programs should be reserved for those who are most impaired.

there is a lack of evidence-based rehabilitation guidelines and that there is no evidence to suggest that facility-based rehabilitation is better than home programs for uncomplicate total knee and hip arthroplasties.

facility-based rehabilitation is still the norm for most patients undergoing uncomplicated knee or total hip arthroplasties, with insurance status being the major determinant of care, despite high-level evidence consistently indicating that facility-based rehabilitation does no better than home-based programs for uncomplicated total knee and hip arthroplasy patients.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the majority of patients undergoing total knee arthroplasty (TKA) and total hip arthroplast (THA) in the Australian public and private sector are still receiving facility-based rehabilitation, even after the evidence has clearly shown that home-based rehabilitation is equally effective.

there is a significant difference in the rehabilitation setting between the two types of insurance, with a greater proportion of public patients being treated with a home-based rehabilitation program.
there is no evidence that facility-based rehabilitation is more effective than home programs for most patients.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the majority of patients with uncomplicated arthroplasty can be safely managed at home.
there is a need to improve the evidence-base for rehabilitation of knee arthroplasty and to implement this in practice.
there is a large variation in the type of rehabilitation provided to patients after knee or hip arthoplasty and this variation is not aligned with evidence.
